targetDefinition: Acute hepatitis C is a newly acquired infection of the liver by hepatitis C virus (HCV) in which viral RNA becomes detectable and hepatic inflammation develops within six months of the presumed exposure. Clinically, it is marked by a rapid rise in serum aminotransferasesâ€”often exceeding ten-fold the upper limit of normalâ€”accompanied variably by fatigue, jaundice, right-upper-quadrant discomfort, or may be entirely asymptomatic; seroconversion with emergence of anti-HCV antibodies usually follows several weeks after RNA detection. The concept encompasses primary, mono-infective, nonâ€“iatrogenic HCV infections of any viral genotype, regardless of symptomatic presentation or peak alanine/aspartate aminotransferase levels, provided chronicity has not been established. It explicitly excludes chronic hepatitis C (persistence of viremia â‰¥6 months), resolved past infections with undetectable RNA, acute exacerbations of known chronic hepatitis C, superinfection on pre-existing liver disease of other etiologies (e.g., hepatitis B, autoimmune hepatitis), and hepatic injury from non-viral causes such as alcohol, drugs, or ischemia.

Acute pancreatitis is a suddenâ€onset inflammatory disorder of the exocrine pancreas characterized by autodigestive injury initiated by premature intrapancreatic activation of digestive enzymes, resulting in rapid acinar cell destruction, interstitial edema, and a sterile or infected inflammatory exudate. The clinical entity is diagnosed when at least two of the following are present: (1) abrupt, severe epigastric pain often radiating to the back; (2) serum amylase or lipase levels equal to or greater than three times the upper limit of normal; or (3) cross-sectional imaging (CT, MRI, or ultrasound) demonstrating pancreatic inflammation, peripancreatic fluid collections, or necrosis. It includes both interstitial-edematous and necrotizing forms and is staged by the Revised Atlanta Classification into mild (no organ failure or complications), moderately severe (transient organ failure <48 h and/or local complications), and severe (persistent organ failure â‰¥48 h). This definition encompasses single, discrete episodes attributable to varied acquired etiologies such as gallstones, alcohol excess, hypertriglyceridemia, post-ERCP injury, drugs, infection, or trauma, but explicitly excludes chronic pancreatitis, autoimmune pancreatitis, asymptomatic hyperenzymemia, pancreatic neoplasms, and recurrent attacks that are components of established chronic pancreatic disease.

Acute respiratory distress syndrome (ARDS) is an acute, non-cardiogenic form of diffuse alveolar injury characterized by rapid onset (within 1 week of a known clinical insult or new/worsening respiratory symptoms) of severe hypoxemic respiratory failure accompanied by bilateral pulmonary infiltrates on chest imaging. Pathologically, it reflects increased pulmonary capillary permeability and diffuse alveolar damage that lead to protein-rich pulmonary edema, surfactant dysfunction, decreased lung compliance, and impaired gas exchange. Diagnostic boundaries are set by the Berlin criteria, which stratify severity as mild (PaOâ‚‚/FiOâ‚‚ 201â€“300 mm Hg), moderate (101â€“200 mm Hg), or severe (â‰¤100 mm Hg) with a minimum positive end-expiratory pressure (PEEP) of 5 cm Hâ‚‚O, and require exclusion of hydrostatic (cardiogenic) pulmonary edema, isolated chronic interstitial lung diseases, chronic obstructive or restrictive disorders, and neonatal respiratory distress syndrome. ARDS encompasses primary (direct pulmonary insults such as pneumonia, aspiration, or inhalation injury) and secondary (indirect systemic insults such as sepsis, pancreatitis, severe trauma) etiologies, but it explicitly excludes chronic or resolving forms once the acute phase has passed, as well as isolated acute hypoxemia without radiographic or physiologic evidence of diffuse alveolar damage.

The concept includes any single or serial measurement of total, unfractionated albumin in serum across all clinical settings, independent of patient age, disease state, nutritional status, timing relative to meals, or acuity of illness. Alcohol dependence is a chronic, relapsing neuro-behavioral disorder characterized by compulsive, maladaptive consumption of ethanol that produces neurobiological tolerance, a definable withdrawal syndrome upon reduction or cessation, and persistent loss of control over intake despite adverse physical, psychological, or social consequences. The condition is acquired after sustained, repetitive exposure to alcohol and is operationalized clinically by meeting diagnostic criteria for moderate or severe alcohol use disorder (DSM-5) or alcohol dependence syndrome (ICD-10), typically demonstrated through features such as craving, unsuccessful attempts to cut down, significant time spent obtaining or recovering from alcohol, and continued use in hazardous situations. Inclusion encompasses patients with documented physiological dependence, those receiving pharmacologic maintenance or relapse-prevention therapy (e.g., naltrexone, acamprosate, disulfiram), and individuals exhibiting objective signs of withdrawal or high tolerance. Exclusions include isolated acute alcohol intoxication, episodic binge drinking without physiologic dependence, historical dependence in full sustained remission, alcohol abuse/harmful use without tolerance or withdrawal, and dependence on other psychoactive substances.

Alcoholic hepatitis is an acute-on-chronic inflammatory and necrotizing liver condition precipitated by sustained excessive ethanol consumption, characterized histologically by hepatocellular ballooning, steatosis, neutrophil-predominant lobular infiltrates, Malloryâ€“Denk bodies, and varying degrees of pericellular fibrosis. Clinically it manifests with recent onset or worsening of jaundice, tender hepatomegaly, and systemic inflammatory response, accompanied by laboratory evidence of predominantly hepatocellular injury with an aspartate aminotransferase (AST) level typically 50â€“400 IU/L, an AST-to-alanine aminotransferase (ALT) ratio >2, and total bilirubin usually exceeding 3 mg/dL. The entity encompasses mild, moderate, and severe forms stratified by prognostic scores such as the Maddrey Discriminant Function, MELD, or ABIC, and may occur on a background of alcoholic steatosis or pre-existing cirrhosis but is distinct from chronic alcoholic cirrhosis without active inflammation. It explicitly excludes non-alcoholic steatohepatitis, viral, autoimmune, ischemic, or drug-induced hepatitis, isolated alcoholic fatty liver without inflammatory injury, and any hepatic dysfunction primarily due to other systemic or congenital causes.

Artificial ventilation, also termed mechanical ventilation, refers to the application of an external mechanical device to generate cyclic airflow into and out of a patientâ€™s lungs when the individualâ€™s intrinsic ventilatory effort is absent, insufficient, or intentionally suppressed. Ascites is the abnormal, clinically significant accumulation of free fluid within the peritoneal cavity, typically exceeding the trace physiologic film (â‰¤50 mL) that lubricates intra-abdominal organs. The concept encompasses any measurable or detectable volume of serous, chylous, or hemorrhagic peritoneal effusionâ€”whether acute, subacute, chronic, mild, moderate, tense, or refractoryâ€”identified by physical examination (e.g., shifting dullness, fluid wave) or imaging modalities such as ultrasound, CT, or MRI. It includes transudative and exudative fluid profiles irrespective of etiology, covers cases with or without concomitant peripheral edema, and spans the full spectrum from first presentation to recurrent or diuretic-resistant states. The definition expressly excludes normal physiologic peritoneal fluid, encapsulated intra-abdominal collections such as abscesses or pseudocysts, hemoperitoneum due solely to trauma, and abdominal distension attributable to bowel gas, obesity, pregnancy, or solid organ enlargement.

Budd-Chiari syndrome is defined as a spectrum of disorders characterized by mechanical obstruction of hepatic venous outflow anywhere from the small intrahepatic veins through the hepatic veins to the supra-hepatic inferior vena cava up to its junction with the right atrium, resulting in impaired drainage of hepatic blood. It encompasses primary forms in which the obstruction is intrinsic to the vessel lumenâ€”most commonly thrombosis or congenital/membranous websâ€”and secondary forms produced by extrinsic compression or luminal invasion from adjacent tumors, cysts, abscesses, or other masses. The syndrome may present as acute, subacute, or chronic disease, with staging based on the rapidity of onset, degree of portal hypertension, and extent of liver parenchymal injury, but all stages share the requirement of demonstrable venous blockage on imaging, surgery, or pathology. This concept excludes sinusoidal obstruction syndrome (veno-occlusive disease), isolated portal or splenic vein thrombosis without hepatic vein involvement, right-sided cardiac failure or constrictive pericarditis causing passive hepatic congestion, and non-obstructive hepatic vascular malformations.

The syndrome may present as acute, subacute, or chronic disease, with staging based on the rapidity of onset, degree of portal hypertension, and extent of liver parenchymal injury, but all stages share the requirement of demonstrable venous blockage on imaging, surgery, or pathology. This concept excludes sinusoidal obstruction syndrome (veno-occlusive disease), isolated portal or splenic vein thrombosis without hepatic vein involvement, right-sided cardiac failure or constrictive pericarditis causing passive hepatic congestion, and non-obstructive hepatic vascular malformations.

Catheterization of the right heart is an invasive cardiovascular diagnostic procedure in which a flexible catheter is introduced, most commonly via a central vein (e.g., femoral, internal jugular, or subclavian), and advanced sequentially through the right atrium and right ventricle into the pulmonary artery and its branches, often culminating in a pulmonary capillary wedge position. The procedure is performed in a cardiac catheterization laboratory or equivalent sterile environment and allows direct measurement of intracardiac, pulmonary arterial, and pulmonary capillary wedge pressures, assessment of cardiac output and shunt calculations, and collection of blood samples for oxygen saturation profiling. It encompasses both traditional fluoroscopy-guided right heart catheterization and Swanâ€“Ganz catheterâ€“based hemodynamic studies when undertaken explicitly for diagnostic hemodynamic assessment. It excludes isolated central venous catheter placement performed solely for medication or fluid administration, left heart (arterial) catheterization procedures, and percutaneous therapeutic interventions such as balloon valvotomy, device closures, or electrophysiologic ablations. No chronicity or severity grading applies because it is a single procedural event; the definition is agnostic to underlying etiologies (congenital versus acquired cardiac disease) and to bedside hemodynamic monitoring catheters that are not placed under fluoroscopic guidance.

targetDefinition: Cholelithiasis with obstruction is a biliary disorder characterized by the presence of one or more calculi originating within the gallbladder or bile ducts that mechanically impede the normal flow of bile through the cystic duct, common bile duct, or intrahepatic ducts. The condition encompasses both acute and chronic presentations when the obstruction is attributable directly to gallstones, including scenarios with transient or persistent impaction, secondary inflammatory changes (e.g., acute calculous cholecystitis, choledocholithiasis), and consequent biliary stasis or pressureâ€related injury proximal to the blockage. It excludes non-calculous causes of biliary obstruction such as benign strictures, malignant biliary obstruction, parasitic infestations, biliary atresia, or sphincter of Oddi dysfunction, and it does not include cholelithiasis without demonstrable luminal obstruction. Severity is delineated by the degree of ductal dilation, biochemical cholestasis (elevations in serum bilirubin, alkaline phosphatase, or gamma-glutamyl transferase), and presence of complications like ascending cholangitis or gallstone pancreatitis, but the definition remains independent of duration until obstruction is relieved or stone is cleared.

The concept encompasses any serum or plasma assay modalityâ€”including conventional (standard) CRP methods with analytic ranges typically detecting 3â€“1,000 mg/L and high-sensitivity CRP (hs-CRP) methods capable of accurately quantifying levels from approximately 0.1 mg/L upwardâ€”regardless of analytic platform (e.g., immunoturbidimetry, nephelometry, ELISA). It includes both single, point-in-time measurements and serial determinations, covers values reported in any recognized unit of measure (mg/L, mg/dL, mg/100 mL, etc.), and applies across all patient ages, sexes, and clinical settings. The definition explicitly excludes qualitative â€œpositive/negativeâ€ serum protein screens, measurements of other acute-phase reactants (e.g., ESR, ferritin, procalcitonin), and any interpretive clinical categorizations (e.g., low-grade vs. marked inflammation) that are downstream of the raw numeric result itself.

The procedure may be performed without contrast or with oral, rectal, and/or intravenous iodinated contrast agents, and can include single-phase or multiphase (e.g., arterial, portal venous, delayed) acquisitions; these variants remain within the scope of a standard abdominal CT as long as the primary intent is anatomic and structural evaluation rather than specialized angiography or functional imaging. Included are routine, low-dose, emergent, inpatient, outpatient, screening, and follow-up abdominal CT studiesâ€”whether obtained on single-slice or multidetector scannersâ€”provided that the imaged field of view is centered on abdominal viscera, musculature, mesentery, and retroperitoneal structures, with or without minimal overlap into the lower thorax or upper pelvis. Excluded are hybrid modalities (PET/CT, SPECT/CT), dedicated CT angiography of abdominal or thoracic vessels, CT enterography, CT colonography, CT urography, scans restricted solely to the pelvis or chest, intra-operative cone-beam CT, and CT-guided interventional procedures such as biopsies or drain placements.

Disseminated intravascular coagulation (DIC) is an acquired, typically acute systemic disorder characterized by widespread, uncontrolled activation of the coagulation cascade leading to formation of fibrin-rich microthrombi throughout the microvasculature, simultaneous consumption of platelets and clotting factors, and secondary activation of fibrinolysis. Diagnostic hallmarks include thrombocytopenia, prolonged prothrombin and activated partial thromboplastin times, decreased fibrinogen, markedly elevated D-dimer or fibrin degradation products, and evidence of microangiopathic hemolysis on blood smear; these laboratory abnormalities must occur in the appropriate clinical setting and are often scored using validated DIC scales (e.g., ISTH criteria). The definition encompasses acute, fulminant, overt presentations as well as subclinical, evolving forms that meet laboratory thresholds but excludes localized intravascular coagulation, chronic compensated coagulopathies such as chronic DIC secondary to large aortic aneurysm or malignancy, hereditary thrombophilias, and isolated thrombocytopenia without consumptive coagulopathy. DIC is always secondary to an underlying precipitating condition (infection, trauma, obstetric catastrophe, malignancy, severe systemic inflammation, toxin exposure, etc.) but is not itself subdivided by etiology for the purposes of concept set construction; primary congenital deficiencies of anticoagulant proteins (e.g., protein C deficiency) are not classified as DIC. Its severity ranges from early compensated states with modest laboratory derangements to severe decompensated states featuring overt bleeding, organ ischemia, and multi-organ failure.

targetDefinition: An electrocardiographic procedure is any standardized clinical technique that records and documents the heartâ€™s bio-electric potentials from surface or implanted electrodes to generate a time-based graphical representation of cardiac electrical activity (the electrocardiogram). It encompasses single-time-point recordings such as resting 12-lead ECGs and rhythm strips, dynamic or extended recordings such as Holter monitoring, event recorders, and continuous inpatient telemetry, as well as exercise or pharmacologic stress ECGs when the primary data collected are electrical waveforms (e.g., P-wave, QRS complex, ST segment, T-wave). The concept explicitly excludes invasive intracardiac electrophysiology studies, device implantation or programming procedures (e.g., pacemaker or defibrillator interrogation), and imaging-based cardiac assessments such as echocardiography or cardiac MRI, even when those studies capture secondary electrical data. Chronicity, etiology, or severity classifications do not apply directly to the procedure itself; rather, the definition is bounded by the modality (surface or implantable electrode acquisition), the analytic output (raw or interpreted electrocardiogram data), and the absence of concurrent therapeutic energy delivery or structural imaging as the principal intent.

Glasgow Coma Score Total is a standardized quantitative measurement of global consciousness derived by summing the numeric ratings assigned to three independent neurologic response domainsâ€”ocular opening (1â€“4 points), best verbal output (1â€“5 points), and best motor response to stimulus (1â€“6 points)â€”yielding an aggregate score that ranges from 3 (deep coma or brain death) to 15 (fully alert and oriented). The concept strictly encompasses assessments performed in patients aged â‰¥16 years using the original adult scoring rubric at a single point in time, irrespective of etiology, and excludes pediatric modifications, extended motor sub-scales, intubated-patient verbal substitutes, or serial trend analyses. It captures acute or transient alterations in consciousness as well as chronic static levels but does not, by itself, specify the underlying cause, duration, or prognosis of impaired consciousness, nor does it include ancillary neurologic examinations such as pupillary reactivity or brainstem reflexes. Variants influenced by pharmacologic sedation, chemical paralysis, mechanical ventilation, or post-resuscitation hypothermia are excluded unless the score explicitly reflects an unconfounded bedside examination performed with these factors appropriately reversed or accounted for.

It includes any numeric INR valueâ€”sub-therapeutic, therapeutic, or supratherapeuticâ€”obtained from single or serial specimens, irrespective of patient age, anticoagulant exposure, or underlying coagulation status. The definition excludes non-standardized PT ratios lacking ISI adjustment, point-of-care capillary INR devices, qualitative bedside clotting tests, viscoelastic whole-blood assays (e.g., TEG, ROTEM), isolated factor assays, chromogenic anti-Xa measurements, and genetic or molecular tests for thrombophilia; it also does not denote a disease state, treatment decision, or severity stage but strictly represents the laboratory result itself.

Insertion of an endotracheal tube is an invasive airway-establishing procedure in which a sterile, cuffed or uncuffed tubular device is advanced through the oral or nasal cavity, past the vocal cords, and into the trachea under direct or indirect visualization to secure patency of the lower airway and permit assisted or controlled ventilation. The concept encompasses elective or emergent orotracheal or nasotracheal intubation performed in any care setting, irrespective of the laryngoscopic technique (direct, video, fiber-optic, or bougie-assisted) and regardless of subsequent ventilation mode (manual bagging, non-invasive ventilator circuit connection, or placement on mechanical ventilation). It includes single-lumen, double-lumen, wire-reinforced, and subglottic-suctionâ€“enabled tubes inserted trans-laryngeally, as well as re-intubations and tube exchanges that preserve the tracheal route. It explicitly excludes tracheostomy creation or cannula changes, cricothyrotomy, laryngeal mask airway or other supraglottic devices, nasopharyngeal or oropharyngeal airways, and procedures limited to sedation without an endotracheal device. The procedure is acute in nature, does not imply chronic airway access, and is independent of the underlying etiology prompting airway management.

The concept encompasses elective or emergent orotracheal or nasotracheal intubation performed in any care setting, irrespective of the laryngoscopic technique (direct, video, fiber-optic, or bougie-assisted) and regardless of subsequent ventilation mode (manual bagging, non-invasive ventilator circuit connection, or placement on mechanical ventilation). It includes single-lumen, double-lumen, wire-reinforced, and subglottic-suctionâ€“enabled tubes inserted trans-laryngeally, as well as re-intubations and tube exchanges that preserve the tracheal route. It explicitly excludes tracheostomy creation or cannula changes, cricothyrotomy, laryngeal mask airway or other supraglottic devices, nasopharyngeal or oropharyngeal airways, and procedures limited to sedation without an endotracheal device. The procedure is acute in nature, does not imply chronic airway access, and is independent of the underlying etiology prompting airway management.

The concept encompasses both acute and chronic presentations and includes all etiologic categoriesâ€”pre-hepatic (e.g., hemolytic), hepatic (e.g., hepatocellular injury or inherited conjugation defects), and post-hepatic (e.g., cholestatic obstruction)â€”provided the primary manifestation is hyperbilirubinemia leading to tissue deposition. The concept encompasses both adult-to-adult and adult-to-pediatric partial graft transfers, irrespective of graft size (e.g., left lateral segment, extended right lobe) or implantation technique, provided the donor remains alive after donation. It explicitly excludes liver transplants that utilize whole cadaveric organs, split-liver grafts derived from deceased donors, xenotransplantation, auxiliary partial orthotopic transplants intended to coexist with the native liver, and combined multi-organ procedures (e.g., liverâ€“kidney or liverâ€“heart transplantation) when the liver component does not originate from a living donor. The procedure is episodic rather than chronic, may involve single or staged operations (donor hepatectomy followed by recipient implantation within the same operative window), and requires compliance with standard immunological matching and vascular/biliary reconstruction protocols intrinsic to liver grafting.

Percutaneous liver biopsy is an invasive diagnostic procedure in which a cylindrical core of hepatic parenchyma is obtained by advancing a biopsy needle through the intact skin, subcutaneous tissues, and hepatic capsule into the liver parenchyma, usually under image guidance such as real-time ultrasound or computed tomography. The technique is intended to yield histologic architecture adequate for microscopic evaluation of hepatocytes, portal tracts, lobular structures, fibrosis, and infiltrative or storage processes, and it involves a single, discrete tissue acquisition episode rather than continuous sampling. This concept specifically includes core-needle and Tru-Cut-type biopsies performed via the percutaneous route, regardless of gauge size, imaging modality, or use of local anesthesia, but excludes transjugular, endoscopic ultrasound-guided, laparoscopic, or open surgical liver biopsies, as well as fine-needle aspiration cytology that does not retrieve a core specimen. It is agnostic to etiology, disease chronicity, or severity and does not encompass repeat sampling protocols, explant pathology, or non-hepatic tissue biopsies.

targetDefinition: â€œpH of Arterial bloodâ€ is a quantitative laboratory measurement that represents the negative base-10 logarithm of hydrogen ion concentration in a specimen obtained specifically from the arterial circulation (typically radial, femoral, or brachial arteries). It is reported as a unit-less value on a logarithmic scale, with physiologic norms generally ranging from 7.35 to 7.45 at sea level and standard atmospheric conditions; values below 7.35 denote arterial acidemia and values above 7.45 denote arterial alkalemia. The concept strictly encompasses direct or calculated pH measurements performed on arterial whole blood or arterialized capillary samples analyzed by blood-gas analyzers, irrespective of patient age, clinical setting, oxygenation status, or presence of ventilatory support. It explicitly excludes pH measurements of venous or mixed venous blood, capillary blood that has not been arterialized, and pH determinations in other body fluids such as gastric aspirate, urine, cerebrospinal fluid, or tissue biopsies. The definition is agnostic to the underlying etiology of acid-base disturbance (e.g., respiratory vs. metabolic causes), the chronicity or acuity of any associated condition, and does not encompass therapeutic interventions like buffering agents or extracorporeal support.

Prothrombin time (PT) is a quantitative coagulation assay that reports the number of seconds required for recalcified, tissue-factorâ€“activated citrated plasma to form a fibrin clot, thereby assessing the functional activity of the extrinsic and common pathways that depend on factors I (fibrinogen), II (prothrombin), V, VII, and X. The concept encompasses any single laboratory measurement of PT expressed in seconds, percentage activity, or laboratory-specific ratio, irrespective of patient age, clinical setting, or the reagentâ€™s international sensitivity index. It explicitly excludes derived or normalized metrics such as the international normalized ratio (INR), partial thromboplastin time (PTT), thromboelastography parameters, and serial trend interpretations; rather, it captures the isolated, point-in-time analytical result produced by standard clot-based instrumentation. No distinctions in chronicity, etiology, or severity are inherent to the measurement itself, and it is independent of congenital versus acquired coagulopathies, anticoagulant therapy status, or concurrent hepatic or hematologic disorders. Measurements obtained from specialized whole-blood viscoelastic tests, genetic factor assays, or platelet function studies are outside the scope of this definition.

targetDefinition: Pulmonary hypertension is a hemodynamic and pathobiological condition characterized by a sustained elevation of mean pulmonary artery pressure (mPAP) greater than 20 mm Hg at rest, confirmed by right-sided heart catheterization. The definition includes both pre-capillary forms (pulmonary vascular resistance â‰¥3 Wood units with normal pulmonary capillary wedge pressure) and post-capillary forms (elevated wedge pressures), provided they meet the mPAP threshold and are not solely transient, exercise-induced, or attributable to acute events like massive pulmonary embolism or acute respiratory distress syndrome. targetDefinition: Sepsis is an acute, life-threatening syndrome characterized by a dysregulated host response to infection that results in clinically significant organ dysfunction, typically evidenced by a rise in the Sequential Organ Failure Assessment (SOFA) score of two points or more (or pediatric-appropriate criteria). It encompasses infections of bacterial, viral, fungal, or parasitic origin, whether community-acquired or healthcare-associated, and regardless of the primary anatomic focus, provided that the infection precipitates systemic inflammatory, immune, hemodynamic, and metabolic disturbances leading to measurable impairment of at least one organ system (e.g., cardiovascular, respiratory, renal, hepatic, hematologic, or neurologic). Included are cases with or without documented bacteremia, as well as culture-negative sepsis when clinical and laboratory data support an infectious etiology. The concept explicitly excludes: (a) localized infections without systemic organ dysfunction; (b) non-infectious systemic inflammatory response syndrome (e.g., pancreatitis, trauma, burns); (c) the more severe entity of septic shock defined by persistent hypotension requiring vasopressors and lactate >2 mmol/L after fluid resuscitation; and (d) chronic post-septic syndromes or convalescent states after resolution of acute organ injury.

Ultrasonography of abdomen is a non-invasive diagnostic imaging procedure that uses high-frequency sound waves, generated and received by a transducer applied to the abdominal surface, to create real-time two-dimensional or Doppler images of intra-abdominal organs and vascular structures. The study routinely encompasses evaluation of the liver, gallbladder and biliary tree, pancreas, spleen, kidneys and ureters, urinary bladder when distended, abdominal aorta and inferior vena cava, and, when technically feasible, portions of the stomach, intestines, adrenal glands, and retroperitoneum. It is performed with the patient fasting to reduce bowel gas and improve acoustic windows, and may include grayscale, color Doppler, and spectral Doppler components for parenchymal morphology, focal lesions, ductal dilation, free fluid, and vascular flow characterization. This definition excludes specialized sonographic modalities such as endoscopic ultrasound, intraoperative ultrasound, contrast-enhanced ultrasound, obstetric or gynecologic pelvic ultrasound, focused assessment with sonography for trauma (FAST), and non-abdominal point-of-care limited scans. It also excludes follow-up studies explicitly confined to a single organ (e.g., dedicated renal ultrasound) unless conducted as part of a comprehensive abdominal survey, thereby delineating the full-scope, transabdominal examination intended to assess multiple abdominal organs in a single session.

Wilsonâ€™s diseaseâ€”also called hepatolenticular degenerationâ€”is a rare, autosomal-recessive, congenital disorder of copper metabolism caused by pathogenic variants in the ATP7B gene, which impair incorporation of copper into ceruloplasmin and block its biliary excretion. The resulting systemic dysregulation leads to progressive toxic accumulation of copper primarily in hepatic parenchyma and later in extra-hepatic tissues such as basal ganglia, cornea, kidneys, and musculoskeletal system, producing a spectrum that ranges from an asymptomatic biochemical phase to overt hepatic, neurologic, psychiatric, hematologic, and musculoskeletal manifestations. Diagnostic hallmarks include persistently low serum ceruloplasmin (<20 mg/dL in most laboratories), elevated 24-hour urinary copper excretion (>100 Âµg), elevated or pathognomonic hepatic copper concentration (>250 Âµg/g dry weight) on biopsy, and characteristic Kayserâ€“Fleischer rings on slit-lamp examination; genetic confirmation of biallelic ATP7B mutations solidifies the diagnosis. The definition encompasses all clinical stages (presymptomatic, hepatic, neurologic, or mixed) and severities (including compensated cirrhosis and fulminant presentations) attributable to inherited ATP7B dysfunction, while explicitly excluding heterozygous carrier status, secondary or acquired copper overload (e.g., cholestatic disorders, excessive supplementation), isolated low ceruloplasmin without copper accumulation, and other hereditary metabolic liver diseases such as hemochromatosis or alpha-1 antitrypsin deficiency.
